p.x:
Good review. Aging is primarily a cybernetic phenomenon: a complex systems communication and control problem. 

Homeostasis degradation is a useful framing.

comments.x: @johnsonmxe Are you aware of @drmichaellevin's theory on aging as a loss of purpose? He talks about it here: https://t.co/YlaQGlzTyU and the paper is here: https://t.co/erlYKDfdeP

p.x:
Given how intimately our minds are coupled with our biophysics it should be at least a little surprising that nobody has figured out how to live forever.

Many processes we think of as “mental” are actually intricately coordinated molecular dances — mind is a core governing factor over metabolism, immunity, even morphology, sometimes at a very high level of resolution.

“Eternal life through internal energy work” is a trope that surfaces regularly across most somatic lineages. Roughly 117 billion humans have been born so far; 109 billion have already died. No one has verifiably reached 123 years, and somatic guilds seem roughly normally represented among centenarians. This is not a good sign for the ‘mind over matter’ anti-aging paradigm.

But the idea that some remarkably effective mental longevity protocol could exist is not completely ridiculous in principle: some people do seem to age much slower due to some mental attitudes (positivity & enjoyment seem useful, holding grudges & ruminating seem bad); others have demonstrable extreme access over various somatic processes (e.g. Wim Hof, various lineages); we have what are probably good intuitions about what psychological states lead to accelerated vs reduced aging. Perhaps modern civilization allows fresh combinations of material surplus, scientific knowledge, and massive parallel search for approaching radical longevity through mental practices. If such a protocol to reverse aging through “energy work” did exist, what would it look like?

My sense is:
(1) any plausible mental protocol would be an add-on to our best physical longevity protocol, eg this wouldn't replace @bryan_johnson's processes; and
(2) the mental/somatic practices should specifically connect with categories of things we know go wrong in aging.

Our models of aging are surprisingly contentious. The big divide in aging research is generally between the “aging as damage” camp vs the “aging as programmed” camp. I began my journey firmly believing in the former (e.g. SENS) but honestly speaking seeing @ydeigin’s thoughtful genomic analysis of covid-as-probably-engineered in April 2020 got me to pay attention to his “aging as programmed” side too.

The vision of the “aging as damage” crowd is that there is a finite list of the types of damage we accumulate over time; fix every item on this list and we fix aging. An adapted mental protocol might involve things like “do X mental practice to clear advanced glycation products; do Y mental practice after applying this special cream to dissolve bioelectric blocks & reinflate the local metabolic repertoire; your resting mental stance should periodically pulse Z, to slowly regenerate telomeres.” More broadly, if there are finite types of aging damage, perhaps at least some people have the latent capacity to learn each of their phenomenological ‘tastes’ and go the other way.

Meanwhile the observation of the “aging as programmed” camp is that we seem to have stepwise, ratchet-like physiological programs, these programs ultimately lead to senescence, and cells airdropped into a body will quickly adapt to its current program. Therefore we need to figure out how to reprogram bodies, not just individual cells and tissues. The foundation for a mental protocol adapted to this observation could be something like “every developmental stage involves a collapse of somatic possibility; staying in a developmental stage requires sustaining the felt-sense possibility of that stage. Functionally, this requires the protection & stewardship of a certain kind of phenomenological & perceptual innocence.” Peter Pan syndrome for your cells & organs.

I doubt that “eternal life through internal energy work” is tractable for any human alive today. But if I think about “what somatic protocols could a superintelligent Dyson sphere create and download into a human nervous system” I’m not going to say it’s theoretically impossible; post-singularity longevity could be different for humans even if our hardware remains completely unchanged.

(90% play, 35% serious)
